title: PointCast Puzzle Studio — Business and Design Study
status: Editorial planning material. No inventory, supplier contract, checkout, class enrollment, partner commitment, or production readiness is claimed.
summary: Start by curating reputable puzzle buying links and publishing ten art concepts. Use a small proof-and-playtest sprint to learn which two deserve production. Compare direct retail, wholesale, licensing, and a later repeat-delivery model using the same honest cost vocabulary.
disclosure: All business numbers below are illustrative US-dollar planning assumptions as of 3 October 2026, except separately cited published supplier/carrier/payment-provider terms. They are not supplier quotations, market averages, offers, or forecasts. Tax, financing costs, founder salary, ongoing overhead, unbudgeted tooling, and larger-market compliance work require separate estimates. No purchase or supplier outreach occurred.

businessModels.title: Curated PointCast store shelf
businessModels.audience: People looking for a first puzzle, a gift, art-led brands, large-piece formats, or a maker resource.
businessModels.offer: External editorial links to real sellers, alongside explicitly labeled original concepts.
businessModels.operations: Check links and product descriptions; show the seller's name; disclose that seller checkout, stock, shipping, and returns are external.
businessModels.economicLogic: This stage earns trust and reveals interest without pretending PointCast has stock. Count qualified outbound clicks only if privacy-preserving analytics are already authorized. There is no commission unless a real agreement is signed and disclosed.
businessModels.evidenceToAdvance: Collect voluntary feedback on art preference, preferred piece count, usable table size, and price with shipping. Interest is a signal, not an order.

businessModels.title: A proof sprint before inventory
businessModels.offer: Select two concepts from the ten and compare physical proofs with different piece-count or finish options.
businessModels.operations: Budget proof orders, shipping, a small artwork revision, playtest compensation/access needs, and a replacement proof. Reserve time to assemble every sample completely.
businessModels.economicLogic: Treat proof costs as research, not saleable inventory. A pretty full image cannot establish cut quality or whether each small piece has useful clues.
businessModels.evidenceToAdvance: A complete piece count, no unacceptable false fits/delamination, readable print, and feedback from beginner and experienced solvers plus people who choose large pieces.

businessModels.title: A 25–75-unit pilot
businessModels.audience: An existing small audience willing to pay for a carefully finished art product.
businessModels.offer: One or two adult-oriented puzzle designs; limited batch scope announced only after proofing and verified supplier capacity.
businessModels.economicLogic: The small pilot can lose money while producing valuable learning. In this illustrative base case, selling all 50 units leaves a $582.25 launch deficit. Set a learning-budget cap before ordering.
operationalNeeds: One verified written specification and sample approval
A realistic delivery window and refund mechanism before any paid preorder
Time for support, missing-piece claims, packing, and address corrections
Separate product-page labeling for prototype, concept, preorder, and in-stock status
businessModels.unknowns: The planned batch range is not a supplier MOQ. Artwork price, piece count, box branding, shipping, tax, and lead time remain unquoted.

businessModels.title: A 250–500-unit direct retail edition
businessModels.offer: One validated 500-piece design with retail box, reference insert, a practical mailer, and a clear missing-piece process.
businessModels.economicLogic: Existing-audience direct sales leave more room than wholesale, but postage, defects, marketing, and unsold inventory can absorb the margin. The worked case below has no paid acquisition; adding it changes the outcome sharply.
businessModels.evidenceToAdvance: Actual paid demand, quote-level landed cost, a passed proof and shipment test, funded support and insurance, and a plan for the unsold portion of the lot.
businessModels.unknowns: Custom tooling, tests, imports/duties, carton storage, tax, and operator salary can exceed these illustrative ranges.

businessModels.title: Wholesale to independent shops
businessModels.audience: A small set of gift shops, museum-style shops, bookshops, or design retailers; none is committed.
businessModels.economicLogic: The example assumes trade revenue equals half the suggested retail price for teaching. It is not a universal retailer rule. At $5 contribution, 500 sold wholesale units do not cover $4,500 fixed launch costs.
contractQuestions: Opening order and reorder quantities; which party pays freight
Payment before shipment versus agreed credit terms
Returns, damaged stock, chargebacks, markdown support, and cancellation
Retail barcode, carton pack, country-of-origin and safety information
No exclusivity or consignment unless its cash exposure is modeled
businessModels.cashRisk: A paper purchase order is not cash. Inventory may be paid before shipment, and credit sales may settle much later. Model bad debt and late payment separately.

businessModels.title: License the art to an established publisher
businessModels.offer: A rights-cleared, proofable artwork pack and documented intended audience/format; publisher would handle manufacturing under a real agreement.
businessModels.economicLogic: Every number is a negotiated-contract scenario, not an industry norm or promised revenue. A royalty percentage means little without its precise sales base, deductions, territory, term, reporting, and audit rights.
contractQuestions: What expressive work and rights are actually owned, including AI-assisted material
Exclusivity, territory, formats, term, print-run approval, and minimum performance
Royalty base and permitted deductions; whether an advance is recoupable
Reporting cadence, audit, payment deadlines, source-file control, returns reserve
Unused-stock sell-off period, reversion, and quality approvals
businessModels.boundary: No publisher has accepted these concepts, and generated pixels are not automatically an exclusive copyrighted asset.

businessModels.title: A quarterly puzzle letter
businessModels.offer: One approved puzzle plus a short original field letter every quarter; a nonrecurring option should remain available.
businessModels.economicLogic: Recurring cash brings recurring obligations. Measure completion, storage burden, repeat demand, skips, churn, and support load before planning multiple deliveries.

retentionExercise.disclosure: A teaching formula with constant per-quarter retention, no discount rate, no capacity limits, and no evidence of real retention.
retentionExercise.formula: Expected shipments = 1 / (1 − quarterly retention); expected contribution = shipments × $11.982, before acquisition and fixed cost.

businessModels.operations: Forecast cash per shipment; keep a refund reserve; communicate delivery windows; provide explicit recurring terms, informed consent, skips, and a simple cancellation path; check current applicable laws before launch.

unitEconomics.title: Work the puzzle before buying the lot
unitEconomics.definition: Contribution is receipts before sales tax minus costs that vary with an order. It is not net profit. Break-even units = fixed launch cost / positive contribution, rounded up.
unitEconomics.numericPolicy: Calculations retain full precision, then format dollars to cents. The published fee input is 2.9% + $0.30; the fee applies here to product plus shipping, excluding tax for simplicity. Real charged tax also affects fees. Purchase taxes and recoverable tax treatment need separate analysis.

assumptions.batchPlanningOnly: 250–500 units; no supplier MOQ or availability is implied.

costNotes.definition: Puzzle plus retail box/reference insert delivered to the operator; a real quote must include or separately model factory price, inbound freight, duties, defects, and nonrecoverable tax.
Outer shipping package; the retail box is already in landed product, so it is not counted twice.
Illustrative paid picking, packing, labeling, and shipment preparation labor; this is not unpaid founder time.
An assumed carrier cost, not a quote. Weigh and measure the packed sample and calculate actual origin-to-destination charges.
A planned compensation input, not a signed royalty contract. If art is paid entirely up front, adapt this line and the fixed budget consistently.
A pooled per-sale allowance for replacements, refunds, extra shipping, and support. It is not an asserted return-rate benchmark; avoid also subtracting the same expected losses elsewhere.
Paid promotion or attributable acquisition spend divided by acquired orders. Zero only means the example assumes an existing audience and excludes paid acquisition.

fixedLaunchBudget.label: Artwork preparation / licensed or human-authored contribution
Product photography / store and service setup
Administration / insurance / rights and compliance estimate

unitEconomics.fixedBudgetLimit: The $4,500 total is an assumed launch budget. It does not establish adequate coverage for legal work, mandated laboratory testing, a custom die, or manufacturing a new format. Replace these placeholders with scoped quotes. Ongoing overhead and operator salary are not included.

sensitivity.label: Base: existing audience; no paid acquisition
Free shipping while keeping the $32 product price
Replacement and return reserve rises to $3
Combined stress: $28 price; $14 goods; $11 postage; $5 acquisition; $3 reserve
Favorable planning case: $40 price; $8 goods; $7 postage; $0.75 reserve; no paid acquisition

inventoryCash.disclosure: Assumes all inventory is paid up front; other variable costs are paid only as sales occur. Reserves are treated as cash set aside. No credit terms, tax, debt, ongoing overhead, or markdowns. Unsold stock is valued at assumed landed cost and may need write-down.
inventoryCash.lesson: The 332-unit contribution break-even is lower than the 401-unit cash-recovery threshold because the full lot was paid for, including the unsold units. Buying more cheaply can still require more cash and leave more waste.

excludedCosts: Ongoing studio rent, software, insurance, and support capacity beyond the assumed launch budget
Founder salary and general management time beyond the handling line
Custom tooling or major new compliance work
International shipping, duties, and international returns

onePageBusinessPlan.heading: Audience and job
onePageBusinessPlan.prompt: Who wants this image, in what setting, and why would they choose a puzzle rather than a print or book?
onePageBusinessPlan.deliverable: One primary audience; occasion; table footprint; preferred format; five observed needs.

onePageBusinessPlan.heading: Product promise
onePageBusinessPlan.prompt: What experience does the image, piece plan, finish, and reference aid create?

onePageBusinessPlan.deliverable: A dated cash schedule, reserve, sell-through scenarios, and storage/waste plan.

onePageBusinessPlan.deliverable: Paid time budget for art approval, QA, packing, accessibility, customer service, and bookkeeping.

onePageBusinessPlan.deliverable: A bounded experiment with budget cap, success criteria, failure criteria, and decision owner.

operations.title: Materials and waste are part of the design
actions: Request paper/board, ink, adhesive, coating, bag, box, and insert composition in writing.
Compare durable reusable packaging with package weight and freight cost; avoid an oversized premium box without a reason.
Track production spoilage, trim waste, damaged cartons, replacements, and unsold stock as separate quantities.
Ask whether offcuts and coated/laminated materials enter real local recovery streams.
Prefer precise substantiated material descriptions over broad eco-friendly claims.
operations.exercise: Make a bill of materials with mass in grams. Estimate waste at assumed 2%, 5%, and 10% spoilage, then replace with observed factory and fulfillment data.

operations.title: Test the assembled object and the shipped box
actions: Approve a complete full-size printed-and-cut proof, not just a digital mockup.
Count and assemble every piece; record false fits, fit pressure, dust, bent tabs, image adhesion, delamination, and loose edges.
Check dark areas and delicate textures under ordinary room light and glare; compare screen art to the physical print.
Ask diverse solvers to locate pieces without relying on color alone; look for shape and image landmarks.
Weigh and measure the packed parcel; run a practical drop/compression/moisture-risk trial and re-inspect the contents.
Keep batch identifiers and a retained sample; define defect acceptance with the manufacturer before production.
operations.boundary: These practical quality exercises do not substitute for mandated safety tests or an accredited laboratory.

operations.title: Age grading follows the actual product
actions: Document intended user, piece dimensions, materials, added accessories, packaging, and marketing.
Do not use an adult label to bypass a child-oriented product's classification.
Identify applicable US safety requirements and responsibility for testing/certification before sale.
Keep warnings and required online advertising notices consistent with actual classification.
Treat any children's edition, wooden pieces, magnets, coatings, or bundled accessories as a new product review rather than recycling a cardboard-puzzle assumption.

operations.title: Promise a delivery you can support
actions: Use measured parcel weight/dimensions and destination mix for carrier budgeting.
Set production, inspection, packing, and dispatch buffers; distinguish dispatch estimates from delivery estimates.
Document address corrections, failed delivery, loss, damaged arrival, and international exclusions.
Fund support time and a replacement reserve; retain enough stock for missing-piece or full-puzzle replacement where feasible.
Before any paid preorder, establish a reasonable shipment basis and the required delay-consent/refund process.

operations.title: Write a missing-piece and returns policy before launch
actions: Separate ordinary change-of-mind returns, personalized customer mistakes, manufacturing defects, damage, and missing pieces.
Tell buyers how to make a claim and what photos/order/batch data are useful; keep the process proportionate.
Budget a complete replacement where a single piece cannot be matched safely to the cut batch.
Confirm who pays return freight and whether supplier credits arrive before customer refunds.
Do not copy a custom manufacturer's no-return policy onto a general retail product.

operations.title: Keep art provenance next to the cost sheet
actions: Use original art, confirmed public-domain material, or a written license for puzzle merchandise.
Record creator, source URL/file, license scope, modifications, consent for recognizable people/property, and restrictions.
Keep human-authored composition, typography, editing, and process records for AI-assisted concepts.
Avoid brand characters, album artwork, lyrics, contemporary art imitations, and unexplained trademarks.
Distinguish permission to use an image from exclusive copyright ownership and from a manufacturer's printing terms.

curriculum.title: Puzzle Product Studio: a business and design concentration study outline
curriculum.label: Proposed editorial study outline, available to follow privately. It is not a new accredited program, enrollment offer, named partnership, or claim that students have completed the work.
curriculum.frame: Use one of the ten original concepts as the same case across six modules. Business asks whether the promise can be sustained; design asks whether assembling the image fulfills that promise.
curriculum.pacing: Six self-guided modules at any pace; roughly 90–150 minutes each, with an optional longer physical proof exercise.
curriculum.access: No account, purchase, supplier contact, public post, live attendance, or payment is required. Digital/paper mockups and supplied hypothetical scenarios are sufficient. Physical sample testing is an optional later extension.
curriculum.finalOutcome: A private product dossier with an original puzzle direction, format/access rationale, print proof plan, rights/material record, channel comparison, base/stress unit economics, and a proceed/revise/stop memo.

modules.title: Who is the puzzle for?
modules.businessQuestion: Which occasion, need, and buyer makes this product worth making?
modules.designQuestion: What image clues welcome that solver?
modules.activity: Choose one concept and write a primary-audience card. Compare a beginner with a confident solver and a solver who prefers large pieces. Record table size, lighting, hand comfort, desired session length, and image preferences without medical promises.
modules.noContactAlternative: Use these hypothetical profiles: A wants a shared table activity with low-pressure stopping points; B likes sorting detailed architecture; C wants larger pieces and clear texture/shape clues.
modules.receipt: Audience card, three needs, two unresolved assumptions, and one optional interview plan.

modules.title: Compose an image people can assemble
modules.businessQuestion: What makes this edition distinct enough to choose?
modules.designQuestion: Where do color, texture, direction, and object landmarks make pieces identifiable?
modules.activity: Divide a concept into a 6×4 study grid. Label distinctive zones and repeated textures. Identify three ambiguous regions. Compare a 300-piece large-piece edition with a 500-piece edition at the same finished size.
modules.designTools: Use a paper grid or any image editor. Inspect at estimated physical piece size, not only as a full-screen poster. Add shape and luminance differences where color is doing all the work.
modules.receipt: A revised composition map, piece-count rationale, reference-aid plan, and a short challenge description.

modules.title: From pixels to a proofable object
modules.businessQuestion: What exactly does the supplier need to quote?
modules.designQuestion: What must survive printing, cutting, packaging, and shipping?
modules.activity: Draft a specification: finished dimensions, target piece count and approximate piece size, board/finish preference, artwork file size, packaging/insert, quantity options, age intent, dispatch destination, and proof approval. Use the supplier's actual template when available rather than inventing universal bleed values.
modules.noPurchaseAlternative: Mark a paper mockup with a border/safe area and simulate seams across tiny text, faces, and landmarks. Create a bill of materials with unknowns left visible.
modules.receipt: Specification sheet, physical-proof checklist, and list of questions awaiting a written quote.

modules.title: Price the delivered experience
modules.businessQuestion: What remains per order, and how much cash must be committed before sales?
modules.designQuestion: Which package choices increase freight or protect quality?
modules.activity: Use the supplied $32 + $7 case. Recompute contribution after $5 acquisition, $11 postage, and a $3 replacement reserve. Compare contribution break-even with the cash recovery of the paid 500-unit lot.
modules.worksheet: Receipts − landed product − mailer − handling − postage − compensation − payment fees − reserve − acquisition = contribution. Divide fixed cost by positive contribution; if contribution is zero/negative, increasing units cannot cure it.
modules.receipt: Base and stress sheet, maximum cash exposure, and a packaging change with its cost/quality tradeoff.

modules.title: Channels, rights, and aftercare
modules.businessQuestion: Who sells, manufactures, holds inventory, and absorbs returns?
modules.designQuestion: What information makes the box and product page trustworthy?
modules.activity: Compare direct retail, one wholesale scenario, and one licensing scenario. Draft a product card that shows status, finished dimensions, intended audience, piece plan, art credit, material information, and seller/returns context.
modules.boundaryExercise: Explain why a label alone does not decide child-product classification and why generated art does not automatically grant exclusive copyright.
modules.receipt: Channel responsibility map, rights ledger, truthful product card, and missing-piece service outline.

modules.title: Publish the decision, not the fantasy
modules.businessQuestion: What evidence supports proceeding, revising, or stopping?
modules.designQuestion: Does the final dossier reveal the actual user experience?
modules.activity: Assemble the dossier. Distinguish confirmed observations, published supplier terms, original decisions, and unknowns. Write a 150-word decision memo with a budget cap and next test. A stop or revision decision can be the strongest outcome.
modules.receipt: Private dossier, six evidence notes, and proceed/revise/stop memo. Optionally publish a rights-cleared case study without personal participant data.

assessment.standard: Shows specific user needs, format tradeoffs, readable cues, and an equivalent private/no-purchase path.
Composition map, piece-plan rationale, proof criteria, and packaging choices agree.
Costs are labeled, formulas are correct, negative contribution is recognized, and unsold inventory is included.
Provenance and product classification questions are explicit; no unearned safety, eco, or partnership claims.
The memo separates evidence from assumptions and proposes a bounded next test.

sections: The audience and why this art was selected

pilotDecisionGates.go: A defined audience and observed willingness to pay for the delivered product.
pilotDecisionGates.reviseOrStop: Only compliments, undated market-size claims, or interest with no price/shipping context.

pilotDecisionGates.go: Rights ledger, understandable piece cues, and full-size proof reviewed by different solver preferences.
pilotDecisionGates.reviseOrStop: Unclear image permissions, excessive repeated texture, unreadable print, or inaccessible piece/box information.

pilotDecisionGates.go: A written scoped quote, approved proof, realistic capacity/lead time, and an accountable quality process.
pilotDecisionGates.reviseOrStop: An assumed MOQ, a generic price screenshot, or no final print-and-cut sample.

pilotDecisionGates.go: Positive contribution under a plausible stress case and a funded learning/inventory/cash cap.
pilotDecisionGates.reviseOrStop: A profitable base case that depends on free labor, no defects, free shipping, or selling every unit immediately.

pilotDecisionGates.go: Documented product classification, required testing, truthful material claims, dispatch/refund process, and support capacity.
pilotDecisionGates.reviseOrStop: Unassigned manufacturer/importer responsibilities, no missing-piece policy, or unsupported safety/ecological claims.

sources.title: SBA — Plan your business
sources.supports: Customer research, competitive analysis, startup cost planning, and business-plan structure. The page distinguishes lean and traditional planning; it does not validate puzzle demand or any PointCast forecasts.

sources.title: Stripe — US pricing
sources.supports: Standard domestic-card fee displayed as 2.9% plus $0.30 per successful transaction. This is a comparison input, not an implemented PointCast payment provider. International cards, conversion, disputes, extra products, and country-specific pricing can differ.

sources.title: USPS — Ground Advantage
sources.supports: Charges depend on package weight, dimensions, and zone. Commercial rates may differ from retail. The service's advertised delivery estimate is generally 2–5 days, with exceptions; no exact PointCast shipping quote was calculated.

sources.title: USPS — Notice 123 price list
sources.supports: Page displays an effective date of July 12, 2026. Use the actual packed weight, dimensions, origin, destination, and available service before replacing the model's assumed $8 postage.

sources.title: puzzleYOU — Wholesale and corporate gifts
sources.supports: Typically 20 puzzles of one size/image sent to one destination qualify for wholesale. A sample may be ordered as one unit. The page lists a typical 1–3-week lead time from purchase, retains its box logo, and says wholesale is unavailable during peak holiday season. Price requires an inquiry; none was made.

sources.title: puzzleYOU — Custom photo jigsaw puzzle catalog
sources.supports: Catalog advertises custom products starting at $29.99 and 48–2000-piece options. This starting retail price is not a quote for a 500-piece PointCast puzzle, wholesale pricing, freight, or a specific box configuration.

sources.title: puzzleYOU — Manufacturing
sources.supports: Supplier says standard puzzles and gift boxes are produced in Williamsport, Pennsylvania using materials sourced from Europe; some specialty products are made by its European sister company. These are supplier claims, not PointCast verification or a domestic-material claim.

sources.title: puzzleYOU — Return policy
sources.supports: Supplier excludes ordinary returns for personalized products but describes replacement for missing pieces, shipping damage, and supplier defects, generally requested within 90 days. This illustrates why a custom supplier's policy is not a complete PointCast retail returns policy.

sources.title: CPSC — Children's products
sources.supports: Classification considers intended use, marketing, consumer recognition, and age guidelines. A printed age label alone does not determine classification. Children's products are primarily intended for ages 12 and younger; applicable testing/certification must be evaluated for the actual product.

sources.title: CPSC — Toy safety business guidance
sources.supports: CPSC lists ASTM F963-23 for toys manufactured after April 20, 2024. The applicable sections depend on the product. Children's toy testing and certification differ from the standard's under-14 scope; review the product's actual intended age and components.

sources.title: CPSC — Small parts business guidance
sources.supports: Explains the small-parts ban for relevant products intended for under-three-year-olds, warnings on certain children's products and ads, certification, and exclusions. Do not assume all cardboard puzzles are exempt or that a generic warning settles the analysis.

sources.title: FTC — Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
sources.supports: A seller needs a reasonable basis for its shipping promise. Without a stated timeframe, the general rule is 30 days. Delays require the specified consent/refund process. These obligations matter before accepting preorder money; a prototype is not evidence of delivery capacity.

sources.title: FTC — Environmental claims: Green Guides summary
sources.supports: Recycled-content and recyclability claims must be specific and supported. Unqualified recyclability requires appropriate facilities available to at least 60% of consumers or communities where sold; packaging, coatings, adhesives, and location can affect the claim.

sources.title: U.S. Copyright Office — AI copyrightability report announcement
sources.supports: Copyrightability of AI-assisted work depends on sufficient human expressive authorship; prompts alone do not establish it. Maintain original source files, human edits, asset permissions, and process notes; do not promise exclusive copyright in unmodified generated pixels.

sources.title: FTC — Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act
sources.supports: Section 4 addresses online negative-option offers: clear material terms, express informed consent, and a simple way to stop recurring charges. This is one federal baseline; state and other applicable rules still need checking before any subscription launch.
